📝我的行程
第1️⃣天：落地海拉尔机场，落地时间早领队安排去阿尔山，落地时间晚就在海拉尔休息第二天出发！
·
第2️⃣天：一整天深度玩转阿尔山秋景，早起看不动河的晨雾，河流边还有牛牛和漫山遍野的金黄橙红交织，午后光线柔和林间光影刚好，随手拍出森系治愈大片
·
第3️⃣天：阿尔山前往呼伦湖再到满洲里住宿，沿途是满目鎏金秋色，中午抵达呼伦湖，秋日湖面澄澈静谧小羊门悠闲踱步，傍晚抵达满洲里，逛异域风情街头，吃地道的内蒙火锅
·
第4️⃣ 天：从满洲里往呼伦湖解锁美丽的风车秋色，在呼伦湖荡秋千欣赏静谧的湖水，沿途前行抵达186彩带河，登高俯瞰蜿蜒曲折的额尔古纳河，傍晚抵达黑山头，赴一场草原绝美日落，晚餐吃当地特色的烧烤
·
第5️⃣天：从黑山头前往恩和俄式的童话乡村，彩色木刻楞小屋搭配秋日田园，满满的异域田园风情，午后打卡整片金黄白桦林秋风落叶氛围感拉满，一路游玩抵达额尔古纳休息，领队带我们去吃了牛排锅地道好吃
·
第6️⃣天：上午欣赏额尔古纳草原初秋的湿地黄绿渐变河道蜿蜒，成群的牛马过水美的不像话，下午奔赴莫日格勒河俯瞰天下第一曲水壮阔又温柔，在落日余晖下我们疯狂拍照记录下开心时刻，返回海拉尔吃了心心念念的俄餐
第7️⃣天：自由行简单逛逛，吃地道的内蒙火锅，然后返程
·
Day1：海拉尔→阿尔山
Day2：阿尔山不动河→阿尔山国家森林公园

Day5：黑山头→恩和民族乡→白桦林→额尔古纳
Day6：额尔古纳→湿地→莫日格勒河→海拉尔
Day7：海拉尔→返程
·

items.title: Tim Willits doesn't think Rideshare's generative AI is damaging Saber's reputation
items.author: Julian Benson
items.summary: A few weeks ago, when I spoke with Tim Willits, chief creative officer at Saber Interactive, makers of games like Space Marine 2, SnowRunner, and World War Z,
items.text:
A few weeks ago, when I spoke with Tim Willits, chief creative officer at Saber Interactive, makers of games like Space Marine 2, SnowRunner, and World War Z, the company was dealing with the shitstorm that ensued from their announcement of Rideshare Stimulator.

The game's basically an Uber simulator, with you driving a car around town picking up fares, but Saber drew all kinds of bad attention when a former writer on the game revealed the game featured generative AI (something left undisclosed on the game's Steam page until recently) and CEO Matt Karch responded by attacking the writer in statements to the press. Something he has since apologised for.

So, naturally, we talked about generative AI and the reputational damage – or lack of – when getting caught out using it.

Watch on YouTube

Rideshare will have a main narrative, similar to other simulator games, in which you start your business in a city and grow it up as you complete jobs. Similar to something you would play through in Snowrunner. "All that is written by humans, all the missions are written by humans," Willits tells me. Where the generative AI appears is in Rideshare's Free Ride mode.

In Free Ride, when you pick up a fare, their dialogue will be generated using an LLM. "What we want to do is feed current events, like maybe there's some soccer game, and some ride will get in and talk about it," Willits explains. He says Saber are "using it here in a small part of a small game to test the waters." and that the company are "interested in how AI can help in games."

Willits says Rideshare is the only game in which Saber are using generative AI – "We don't have AI in Space Marine. We don't have AI in Hellraiser. We don't have AI in Jurassic Park, but we want to figure it out and we want to try something."

When I spoke with Willits, the thing I most wanted to know was why there was no AI disclosure on the Rideshare's Steam page when it was first revealed. Valve have a clear policy on disclosing the use of generative AI both in the production of a game and if any feature of the game makes ongoing calls to LLMs.

The reason, Willits says, is they "had an announce plan, but that got a little sideways". There was going to be a sneak peak, then there would have been reveals of the game's features in the future, and as part of that the generative technology would have been revealed. To indicate how early in the game's reveal rollout they are, Willits points out Rideshare's "not here" at Gamescom. "Unfortunately, we had some people talk about the game when they weren't supposed to be talking about the game and that just kind of escalated."

Though, I bring it back to Valve's AI disclosure policy because it doesn't make a distinction between whether a feature has been announced or not, only whether the technology is used in a game. Shouldn't the disclosure still have been there when the game was announced? "Okay, sure," Willits says.

The point I'm building to with Willits is that by not initially disclosing the use of AI, it seeds doubt about generative AI's use in Saber's other games. The tool may have been used but the company is not yet ready to announce or reveal it. I point to another of Saber's games, Road Kings, a new American trucking simulator which I really enjoyed at a preview event in April. While on the road, other drivers or job brokers may message you to ask for help, spurring an emergent quest. Certainly, there's no suggestion that these quests are generated by AI, but to a player the two systems could appear similar and they may now question 'Is this generative AI Saber's not copped to yet?'. "You may be overthinking it a little bit," Willits says. "I wouldn't worry about that. Again, the wishlists are up, interest is up, preorders across our games are up."

I didn't want to move on immediately, as Road Kings captures the issue well. I saw the game back in April but its embargo for the preview only came up after the Rideshare story had broken. I played and enjoyed that game and its mix of American Truck Simulator-style hauling blended with scenes you might see in a disaster move like Twister. But the comments on the preview were largely about the Rideshare news and Saber's use of AI. Willits, again, disagrees this is an issue. "I wouldn't really worry about that," he says. "The games will speak for themselves. You enjoyed Road Kings. The people that play it, they will enjoy it. I've been in the industry for 30 whatever years, you will always get crazy comments."

Willits points back to when he was working at id and they announced Quake 3 would need a video card to play. "We were roasted," he says. "The internet hate was crazy. 'You're ruining the industry. How can you make me pay $100 for a video card?' – imagine a $100 video card! – But the game came out and people liked it."

Willits also points to the launch of Steam, which, while a well-regarded platform now, was not universally loved at launch. In part because its servers struggled and its online functionality demanded more from peoples' internet than a lot of dial up and early broadband connections could provide. "I think we're in a period now of technology change that people are really unsure about," Willits says. "We, as game developers, don't really know what we're doing with it yet. Players don't really know what's going on with it. But I do think that there will be a game from somebody that will be so awesome that everyone will be like 'That's it. Now I get it.' I think the games will speak for themselves and when people play or they read your stories, and they watch the videos and they see the content, they will make their own determination."

As I've said in the past to other developers, I can believe there are ways these new AI technologies could benefit my work. For instance, the first transcription pass of most my interviews is done automatically because I use Google's Recorder app. But I also know the worst thing I could do with [insert AI tool of your choice] would be to generate an article for RPS. No one comes to this site to see something cobbled together by an LLM, they want something lovingly stitched together by these dyslexic typo-spewing hands. So I ask Willits what he thinks the benefit for Saber will be.

"As a game developer, if you're going to try something with brand new generative AI, it's much better to try it with something small [rather] than your biggest title," Willits says. "For us, part of our strategy at Saber is to make our mega hits – Space Marine 3, Jurassic Park, Turok – but we have to have smaller games that are consistent when it comes to how long it takes to make, how much money they make, [that's where] we experiment with things. Look at Spintires. That was an experiment that turned into a mega franchise. Rideshare fits into that category. It is a Rideshare simulator, where you drive around and you pick people up. There's really not much more you can really do there. And so for us, we wanted to be like 'Well, let's try this. Let's try it here because if it doesn't work out, it's on that game. It's not on our mega hits.'"

In the case of Rideshare's Free Ride mode, Willits says "This is a gameplay feature that is not possible without this technology. It would be logistically too hard, it'd be so expensive. We'd have to have an army." And, as he's described it, a mode where passenger dialogue is generated in response to current events fed into the game, I agree. Either you would have a madlibs style system of words being swapped in and out of repeating schemas, or a human writer adding additional lines in response to real world news events.

I do want to see if Saber are able to produce anything better than the other games that have stuck LLMs inside the throats of their characters. In Where Winds Meet, players quickly convinced one of the NPCs that they were pregnant, and another to provide cooking advice for potatoes and ketchup. That implementation and others were panned by developers Samuel Horti spoke to back in December.

My experience of generative AI dialogue has largely been formulaic and predictable. Which, could make for incredibly dreary car journeys. Ironically, the last taxi ride I was in I told the driver he was taking us to an engagement meal and he told me how AI was going to destroy the world by 2030.

Travel and accommodation to Gamescom was provided by the conference organisers.

items.title: 10 Shows To Watch While Waiting For Henry Cavill’s Highlander Reboot
items.author: Misty Layne
items.summary:
Published Sep 19, 2026, 7:01 AM EDT

Misty Layne started as an actor and sketch comedy writer before deciding to concentrate mainly on writing. Utilizing both
items.text:
Published Sep 19, 2026, 7:01 AM EDT

Misty Layne started as an actor and sketch comedy writer before deciding to concentrate mainly on writing. Utilizing both her love of television and film and her behind-the-scenes knowledge, she began a website reviewing films in 2013, with a focus on horror and indie media. Eventually, she began writing about all things television and film for other sites as well. Misty shares a home with five cats, a ton of books, and a fairly impressive vinyl collection.

Highlander was one of those films that came at the perfect time and captured imaginations. The original film spawned several sequels, a handful of television shows, and a novelization. However, a reboot never happened, even though Summit Entertainment announced in 2008 that it was remaking the original movie.

Now, however, the long wait is almost over. Starring Henry Cavill as Connor MacLeod, Amazon MGM's upcoming movie promises everything fans loved about the original, plus serious John Wick energy, as first-look footage for the Highlander reboot revealed at CinemaCon 2026. Since principal photography only began in early 2026, though, it will still be quite a while before the film arrives.

In the meantime, Highlander fans can tide themselves over with other excellent television shows with similar vibes to the original movie, exploring narrative elements like time travel and immortality that made the film such a cult favorite. Not only will catching up with these satisfy the need for some Highlander-esque hijinks, but it'll make the wait for Henry Cavill's Highlander reboot go by that much faster.

Highlander: The Series (1992–1998)

Image via MovieStillsDB

What better show to watch while waiting for the Highlander reboot than Highlander: The Series? (It is the best sequel to the original Highlander film, after all.) Though the series focused on a different character than Connor MacLeod, Christopher Lambert did appear in the first episode as a segue from the films. The protagonist in the show is Duncan MacLeod, an Immortal who has lived for 400 years, but took himself out of the Game by hiding from other Immortals.

Duncan MacLeod's Immortal journey primarily examines his relationships, whether they be with other Immortals or mortals. Throughout the series, he loves and loses people several times, fights numerous others like himself, and learns about the Watchers, a secret society that records the history of the Immortals. Overall, the series shares many themes with the films, but it also reveals more backstory about Duncan and the Immortals in general. While it isn't the same as the Highlander film, Highlander: The Series is the closest someone can get to it while waiting to see Connor MacLeod on the big screen once again.

Forever Knight (1992–1996)

Image via MovieStillsDB

Forever Knight featured Nick Knight, a vampire who was also a detective and was eager to shed his immortality and become human once again. Honestly, in some ways, this show is a bit of a rip-off of Highlander, not only because it features an immortal who wants to become human, but also because the vampires on this show had a warning sense about each other, just as the Immortals do. The show also contains many flashbacks to the main character's previous lifetimes.

However similar the two were, this show stood on its own as a fun urban fantasy show, which followed Nick's struggle to protect innocent people to make up for the sins of his past lives as a killer, while also trying to keep the secrets of the vampire world away from any humans in his life. Unfortunately, Forever Knight's series finale was hated by fans, sparking quite a bit of controversy.

Xena: Warrior Princess (1995–2001)

Sometimes we're simply in the mood for an action-packed melodrama from an earlier decade that's a tad cheesy. Xena: Warrior Princess and Highlander both offer that up in spades. Here, the infamous warrior comes in the form of the haunted heroine, Xena, who hopes to make up for the harm she's caused innocents in the past by helping people now. Xena constantly struggles to fight for the greater good throughout the series, willing to sacrifice everything to be better than the person she previously was.

However, her grand adventures are what most make Xena: Warrior Princess like Highlander. With her trusty sidekick, Gabrielle, at her side, Xena made her way through a fantasy version of Ancient Greece, a sword in hand and her Chakram in the other. In the fight between good and evil, there's no shortage of mortal enemies or battles, after all, and this show delivered all that action in an enjoyable (and occasionally ridiculous) way.

Highlander: The Raven (1998–1999)

Fireworks Entertainment

Highlander: The Raven didn't last long, but it carried on the good-versus-evil themes the rest of the Highlander franchise dealt with. This time, the Immortal was a woman named Amanda, introduced in Highlander: The Series. However, Amanda doesn't start on the side of good; when the show begins, she's a thief. She's also framed for murder, which is how she meets a cop named Nick Wolfe, who soon learns of her immortality.

Amanda's journey is one of redemption, as she spends the series trying to become a better person with Nick's help. She also finds herself facing off against other Immortals and actually battling them, instead of running away as she would have previously. The show offers a different perspective on Immortal life and explores what might make an Immortal something other than good and what could lead them to switch sides. It's an intriguing watch. However, be forewarned: Highlander: The Raven ends not only with a wild twist, but on a cliffhanger.

The Immortal (2000–2001)

Chum Television/ Courtesy: Everett Collection.

Imagine something similar to Highlander, but more martial arts-based, and you'll have The Immortal. This show is a quick watch at only 22 episodes, with a main character similar enough to Connor MacLeod that in the book The American Martial Arts Film, author M. Ray Lott wrote: "The resemblance to Highlander is probably not coincidental." Raphael Cain sees his wife and child murdered in 16th-century Asia by demons, and decides to dedicate his life to pursuing them throughout the centuries with the aid of magic, his squire, and his samurai sword.

Henry Cavill's long-awaited Highlander reboot is finally moving forwards but it needs to take some steps to avoid the franchise's past mistakes.

Related

The show is mostly set in the 21st century, and while it's a bit silly at times, it's also entertaining. Perhaps The Immortal wasn't the best show around (hence the single season), but it makes an excellent replacement for those missing out on the elements that made Highlander what it was.

Angel (1999–2004)

Image via MovieStillsDB

Angel might not seem similar to Highlander at first glance, but since both feature an ancient immortal European who fights evil beings in modern times, they're more alike than one might think. Angel originated on Buffy the Vampire Slayer as a brooding vampire who became Buffy's first love before getting his own spin-off show. There, Angel is still broody, but this time he works as a private investigator, waging a war against the forces of darkness (often in the form of lawyers).

Another thing the two properties share is flashbacks to the past. Angel's life has gone on so long that his early days as Angelus, or even his memories from when he was still human, are vital to understanding what makes him tick in the modern world. He's seen friends, family, and lovers come and go while he lives on, much like MacLeod, but somehow remains standing. He also has more than enough mortal enemies to keep him occupied throughout the centuries. In the end, Angel's dark, tormented, immortal main character has much in common with Highlander's protagonist.

Vikings (2013–2021)

MovieStillsDB

This historical drama might seem like an unlikely choice for those missing Highlander's supernatural shenanigans, but like Highlander, Vikings explores the warrior ethos while delving into concepts of legacy. Both shows also feature farmers who become so much more as they battle personal demons and mortal enemies. Plus, Vikings has epic fight scenes that should satisfy any Highlander fan.

This show draws on the tales of Ragnar Lodbrok, one of the more notable Norse heroes. Over the course of the series, Lodbrok goes from farmer to Scandinavian king, with later seasons following his sons and their adventures. Dramatic and action-packed, Vikings is a fantastic show for those seeking adventure and battles (and who don't mind a few historical inaccuracies).

Outlander (2014–2026)

When it comes to time-traveling epics involving Highland warriors, Outlander is the next best thing after Highlander. Based on Diana Gabaldon's bestselling book series, the show follows a nurse from 1945 who time-travels to 1743 in Scotland, gets dragged into the Jacobite uprising, and falls in love with a Highland warrior. While Outlander has romance at its heart, it's also about fighting for what one believes is right, packed with adventures across eras.

Additionally, the show features a protagonist who struggles with destiny, much like Connor MacLeod. Jamie Fraser and his family constantly try to defy fate, but destiny always arrives. Plus, with eight seasons, Outlander will keep fans plenty busy until the release of the Highlander reboot.

The Witcher (2019–Present)

For those who can't wait to see Henry Cavill swinging a sword again, The Witcher should satisfy that need. Based on the Polish book series of the same name by Andrzej Sapkowski, the show follows Geralt of Rivia (Cavill in seasons 1–3) as a monster hunter in a fantasy world. Like MacLeod, Geralt is long-lived and hard to kill (though he isn't immortal). While there's no time travel involved, The Witcher timeline is sometimes confusing enough that viewers might feel as if it is.

The show is action-packed, as Geralt not only battles monsters but also gets tangled up with Princess Ciri (thanks to the Law of Surprise), Yennefer the witch, court politics, and more. The show shares a similar vibe with Highlander, not only in its battles and sword fights, but also in how its main character wanders the world for centuries. That makes The Witcher a perfect show to rewatch or catch up on before the Highlander reboot comes out.

Highlander: The Animated Series (1994–1996)

Highlander: The Animated Series was a kids' show, but it often dealt with mature and violent themes. It was also very different from most previous iterations in the Highlander universe, set far in the future in a post-apocalyptic society where all Immortals except one had agreed to quit the Game and instead help humanity by preserving its knowledge. Of course, it isn't long before the one who hasn't taken the oath, Kortan, basically takes over the world and, in the process, kills Connor MacLeod. Connor's death, though, allows a future Immortal to rise and take on the challenge of fighting Kortan.

The show explored mentoring new generations and passing on knowledge rather than hoarding it, as well as the eternal personal struggle between good and evil. Unlike most cartoons, the characters in Highlander: The Animated Series aren't one-note; they're multifaceted, with the potential for good or evil, including Quentin, the Immortal who can take on Kortan. Even though it only had two seasons, it's an interesting addition to the Highlander universe and worth a watch.

items.text:
Red Dead Redemption 2's New Ranching Feature Lets You Build Your Own Farm

Published Sep 19, 2026, 7:00 AM EDT

Paul Farrelly is a Contributing Writer for Screen Rant’s Gaming section and the founder of GeekGasm.org, a site dedicated to celebrating all things gaming, from triple A blockbusters to weird and wonderful indie hits. Based in Louth, Ireland, Paul has spent years writing about games, pop culture, and tech, turning his lifelong love of gaming into a career that lets him talk (probably too much) about what makes this industry so endlessly fascinating.
He’s previously written and collaborated with several entertainment outlets, including LADbible, gaining a wide perspective on how gaming fits into today’s pop culture conversation. His work blends genuine enthusiasm with thoughtful analysis, exploring how design, storytelling, and community have made gaming one of the most creative mediums around.
When he’s not glued to a controller or keyboard, Paul’s usually spinning vinyl, plotting his next horror marathon, or debating which Resident Evil entry really reigns supreme.

Red Dead Redemption 2 is almost eight years old but still remains one of the most immersive gaming experiences to ever exist. It's an amazing open world teeming with life and glorious details forces players to slow down and drink it all in. Living the life of a bandit on the run, though, isn't for everyone and many would love to see Arthur Morgan settle down and build a life away from the gunfire. But while most of the spotlight this year is on another upcoming Rockstar game, there's still life left in RDR2.

Not all mods are made equal and when it comes to Red Dead Redemption 2, you can really go down a rabbit hole if you're not careful. Thanks to NexusMods, the Ranching mod for Red Dead Redemption 2 is truly something special. Red Dead Redemption 2 already offers players some escapism through hunting, fishing, herding and looking after your camp. But getting even more content and new ways to play is always welcome when it's as good as this.

NexusMods

The Ranching mod allows players to work on ranches across the world map to earn some extra coin. There are seven locations scattered across the wild west that Arthur can seek work at. Jobs include planting seeds, feeding chickens, spreading hay and refilling water troughs, to name but a few. If gang life and train heists are stressing you out, you can always kick back and earn an honest living for a change. You can even work on McFarlane ranch and drink in some nostalgia for the original Red Dead Redemption game. Getting something for free for Red Dead Redemption 2 is never a bad thing either.

But the main reason this mod is so special is that it allows you to own and run your very own ranch. Forget working for others, Arthur Morgan can carve his own slice of paradise in the world and live out the simple life. You can grow crops to fruition, harvest them, load up your wagon and sell your produce to the locals. Beecher's Hope is expanded for ranching purposes, or you can purchase ranches in three other locations. Argile Rise, Ridge View Cabin, Shepard's Rise Cabin are available to purchase thanks to the Ranching mod.

NexusMods

Roleplaying as either a ranch hand or a ranch owner in Red Dead Redemption 2 is just another great reason to get lost in this amazing world created by Rockstar Games. Stardew Valley crossed with Wild West shenanigans sounds like a perfect balance of calm and chaos. Sure, you could spend your time robbing banks and escaping from the law, but the simple life of raising animals and crowing crops sounds like a peaceful escape inside one of the greatest games of all time.

With November 19th fast approaching, Grand Theft Auto 6 is about to take over most of our gaming lives for a few months at least. So now is the perfect time to jump back into Red Dead Redemption 2 before GTA arrives. Why get in a spot of farming and cattle herding in the Wild West before the neon-soaked Leonidas takes over our TV screens? Ranching mod for Red Dead Redemption 2 is available for free on PC and you can download it today.

If gang life and train heists are stressing you out, you can always kick back and earn an honest living for a change. You can even work on McFarlane ranch and drink in some nostalgia for the original Red Dead Redemption game. Getting something for free for Red Dead Redemption 2 is never a bad thing either.

But the main reason this mod is so special is that it allows you to own and run your very own ranch. Forget working for others, Arthur Morgan can carve his own slice of paradise in the world and live out the simple life. You can grow crops to fruition, harvest them, load up your wagon and sell your produce to the locals. Beecher's Hope is expanded for ranching purposes, or you can purchase ranches in three other locations. Argile Rise, Ridge View Cabin, Shepard's Rise Cabin are available to purchase thanks to the Ranching mod.

Roleplaying as either a ranch hand or a ranch owner in Red Dead Redemption 2 is just another great reason to get lost in this amazing world created by Rockstar Games. Stardew Valley crossed with Wild West shenanigans sounds like a perfect balance of calm and chaos. Sure, you could spend your time robbing banks and escaping from the law, but the simple life of raising animals and crowing crops sounds like a peaceful escape inside one of the greatest games of all time.

With November 19th fast approaching, Grand Theft Auto 6 is about to take over most of our gaming lives for a few months at least. So now is the perfect time to jump back into Red Dead Redemption 2 before GTA arrives. Why get in a spot of farming and cattle herding in the Wild West before the neon-soaked Leonidas takes over our TV screens? items.title: Dune Awakening now has a solo mode for players put off by its MMO leanings, while Funcom has adjusted progression so 'you don't have to lose things anymore'
items.author: Rick Lane
items.summary: Dune Awakening was lauded for its survivalist take on Frank Herbert's sci-fi epic when it was released last year, but there's one element of Funcom's sci-fi
items.text:
Dune Awakening was lauded for its survivalist take on Frank Herbert's sci-fi epic when it was released last year, but there's one element of Funcom's sci-fi adventure that's proved consistently controversial, and that's its MMO-adjacent elements. Players seemingly love constructing bases and braving the many dangers lurking in Arrakis' deserts, but are less keen on sharing that experience with other players, especially when the game becomes more competitive in its PvP focussed Deep Desert.

Now though, in a move that would please Harkonnens galaxy-wide, Funcom has made it so you can keep Arrakis all to yourself. Dune Awakening's long-sought after single-player mode has arrived. Update 1.5 introduces a tweaked version of Awakening suitable for solo play, while also adjusting Arrakis in a bunch of other ways to make it generally more accessible and less punishing.

Funcom has changed several core mechanics to make solo mode work, chiefly retooling multiplayer-reliant systems so they can work independently. The player-driven market known as the Exchange now functions as a sci-fi supermarket offering a wide-array of items for players to pick up as they please. Meanwhile, its Landsraad political system simulates rival guilds automatically, ensuring it "progresses even without player participation". Finally, while not player-driven, Coriolis storms have been softened so that players can maintain progress in the Deep Desert, though Function cautions that these storms remain "very dangerous."

Perhaps the most interesting addition, though, is difficulty settings. Awakening now features three difficulty presets for both single-player and self-hosted servers, alongside a fourth, customisable difficulty mode that lets players tweak parameters like sandstorms, security zones, item durability, base decay and even XP multipliers.

Alongside adding solo play to Awakening, Funcom has also made its multiplayer less confrontational. Multiplayer can now be played wholly PvE. The Deep Desert's PvP is no longer mandatory, while the starting area of Hagga Basin is now exclusively PvE (although you can make it a "full PvP zone" if you run your own server).

This friendlier approach isn't limited to player interactions either. The game itself has been made less punishing in a variety of ways. Bases can be reconstructed wholesale thanks to a new snapshot system that acts as a blueprint for your entire base. Destroyed vehicles can be recovered for up to 30 days after being lost. Base upkeep taxation has been removed entirely, and the durability penalty upon death has been lowered from 5% to 2%.

Funcom summarises the changes with the line "You don't have to lose things anymore," which, while I understand the sentiment, is a little strange given that Arrakis is supposed to be brutally harsh by its very nature. But Dune Awakening is far from the only game currently trending away from friction. Bungie is adding a permanent PvE mode to Marathon, after its uncompromising extraction shooter failed to maintain a large audience. Even in the realm of single-player, The Blood of Dawnwalker's developer has said it may not include a time-limit system in the sequel (which the studio is already working on) after it proved the most controversial element of the otherwise lauded RPG.

I don't know whether this trend toward smoother, more siloed gaming experiences is a positive one, but given the 2010s were dominated by fiercely challenging soulslikes and hyper-competitive battle-royale games, it is interesting. In any case, If the addition of single-player has ignited your interest in Dune Awakening, Funcom's sci-fi survival sim is half-price until October 1.

items.title: Pokémon Officially Unveils Brand-New 30th Anniversary Eeveelution Design
items.author: Angharad Redden
items.summary:
Published Sep 19, 2026, 6:00 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital
items.text:
Published Sep 19, 2026, 6:00 AM EDT

Known as 'Cyberpunk 2077's' biggest fan, Angharad is a Welsh games writer who thrives in anything related to digital storytelling. If a video game explores the intricacies and horrors of womanhood, she is there.
Thanks to previous work at GAMINGbible, GameByte, The Loadout, Game Luster, Angharad has built a strong understanding of both the digital world and what fans want from it and is eager to share her thoughts and expertise with readers.

It is hard to believe that this year celebrates the 30th anniversary of Pokémon. First created back in February 1996 with the release of the Pocket Monsters Red and Green video games in Japan, the franchise, conceived by Satoshi Tajiri alongside illustrator Ken Sugimori, has become a worldwide phenomenon thanks to the launch of cards, movies, television shows, video games, and more.

Perhaps what makes the Pokémon franchise as beloved as it is, is the chance for fans to collect Pokémon trading cards, and with some cards fetching thousands of dollars, it is no wonder that many consider it to be a lucrative hobby.

Now, to celebrate the 30th anniversary of the hit franchise, Pokémon TCG is releasing its 30th Celebration Expansion, with the official description reading as follows:

Celebrate 30 years of joy with fan-favorite Pokémon spanning three dazzling decades! Explore some of the cards offered in the 30th Celebration expansion, and dive into a variety of card collections spanning the past, present, and future of the Pokémon TCG!

Not only that, but according to the small print, all cards available in the 30th Celebration Expansion are now able to be played in official tournaments, so you have no excuse not to check out the latest batch of stunning cardboard, especially as one includes art of an anniversary Eeveelution.

On the official website, we can check out the 154 brand-new designs that have been released, split between five categories: Pokémon Ex, Special Art, Pikachu Rare, Classic Collection, and Futuristic Rare.

Whilst the Futuristic Rare additions include Mew and Mewtwo, there is one addition to the Special Art category that has captured our attention: Sylveon. On this stunning Eeveelution card, we can see the dazzling pink and blue design set across a vibrant burst of colors. Titled 'Colorful Harmony', it will be a stunning addition to your Pokémon TCG collection, and shows us an Eeveelution that we have not yet seen.

Not only that, but we at Screen Rant put together a simple guide of the best Pokémon TCG cards to get as part of the 30th anniversary celebration additions. For Sylveon, we said, "Sylveon ex is a strong card with 270 HP to protect it, but its one attack must be used strategically to be very effective. Colorful Harmony requires players to have several types of Basic Energy attached to Pokémon in order to do a lot of damage. Colorful Harmony states that, "This attack does 50 damage for each type of Basic Energy attached to all of your Pokémon."

"As you obviously would have some Psychic Energy in play, it will at least have base damage of 50. If you plan the use of this card for when there are multiple types applied to cards, it could do upwards of 400 damage."

So, if you want to add a strong card to your Pokémon TCG collection, or you just want to admire this stunning Eeveelution, make sure to check out the 30th anniversary celebration now.

items.title: Jason Statham's Biggest Action Hit Officially Scores a Brand-New Streaming Home
items.author: Chris McPherson
items.summary:
Jason Statham's Biggest Action Hit Officially Scores a Brand-New Streaming Home

Image via PA Images/INSTARimages

Published Sep 19, 2026, 5:40 AM EDT

Chris
items.text:
Jason Statham's Biggest Action Hit Officially Scores a Brand-New Streaming Home

Image via PA Images/INSTARimages

Published Sep 19, 2026, 5:40 AM EDT

Chris is a Senior News Writer for Collider. He can be found in an IMAX screen, with his eyes watering and his ears bleeding for his own pleasure. He joined the news team in 2022 and accidentally fell upwards into a senior position despite his best efforts.
For reasons unknown, he enjoys analyzing box office receipts, giant sharks, and has become known as the go-to man for all things Bosch, Mission: Impossible and Christopher Nolan in Collider's news division. Recently, he found himself yeehawing along to the Dutton saga on the Yellowstone Ranch.
He is proficient in sarcasm, wit, Photoshop and working unfeasibly long hours. Amongst his passions sit the likes of the history of the Walt Disney Company, the construction of theme parks, steam trains and binge-watching Gilmore Girls with a coffee that is just hot enough to scald him.
His obsession with the Apple TV+ series Silo is the subject of mockery within the Senior News channel, where his feelings about Taylor Sheridan's work are enough to make his fellow writers roll their eyes.

Jason Statham is the most dependable and reliable action star of our generation. Every year, a new Statham action movie comes out, and it delivers exactly what we want: a one-man army, a few quips, some cannon fodder bad guys, and the good guy winning in the end. Sometimes, though, these films hit a bit differently and are elevated because something about them is just better than the norm. In 2024, Statham took on what could have been a silly film with David Ayer, but it became something much bigger. Now, a new audience can see it.

More than two years after becoming a surprise theatrical hit, The Beekeeper has officially found a new streaming home on Peacock. The film features Statham as Adam Clay, a deadly ex-operative of a secret government agency called — you guessed it — the Beekeepers. After a cybercrime ring drives his friend to suicide, Clay launches a relentless, violent crusade for justice. Ayer reportedly brought in a retired FBI agent to consult on the movie’s structure and procedural aspects. Meanwhile, Statham, ever the committed performer, took the time to learn about beekeeping and trained hard for the film’s most demanding stunts — most of which he performed himself.

The cast is led by Statham as Adam Clay, alongside Emmy Raver-Lampman (The Umbrella Academy) as FBI Agent Verona Parker, Josh Hutcherson (The Hunger Games) as Derek Danforth, Bobby Naderi (Bright) as Matt Wiley, Minnie Driver (Good Will Hunting) as Janet Harward, Phylicia Rashad (Creed) as Eloise Parker, Jemma Redgrave (Doctor Who) as President Danforth, and Jeremy Irons (Watchmen) as Wallace Westwyld.

Collider Exclusive · Sci-Fi Survival Quiz
Which Sci-Fi World Would You Survive?
The Matrix · Mad Max · Blade Runner · Dune · Star Wars

Five universes. Five completely different ways the future went wrong — or sideways, or up in flames. Only one of them is the world your instincts were built for. Eight questions will figure out which dystopia, galaxy, or desert wasteland you'd actually make it out of alive.

💊The Matrix

🔥Mad Max

🌧️Blade Runner

🏜️Dune

🚀Star Wars

TEST YOUR SURVIVAL →

01

You sense something is deeply wrong with the world around you. What do you do?
The first instinct is often the truest one.

APull on every thread until I understand the system — then figure out how to break it.
BStop asking questions and start stockpiling — food, fuel, weapons. Questions don't keep you alive.
CKeep my head down, observe carefully, and trust no one until I know who's pulling the strings.
DStudy the patterns. Every system has a rhythm — learn it, and you learn how to survive it.
EFind the people fighting back and join them. You can't fix a broken galaxy alone.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

In a world of scarcity, what resource do you guard most fiercely?
What we protect reveals what we believe survival actually requires.

AKnowledge. If you understand the system, you don't need resources — you can generate them.
BFuel. Everything else — movement, power, escape — runs on it.
CTrust. In a world of fakes and informants, a truly reliable ally is rarer than any commodity.
DWater. And after water, information — the two things empires are truly built on.
EShips and credits. The galaxy is big — you survive it by being able to move through it freely.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What kind of threat keeps you up at night?
Fear is useful data — if you're honest about what you're actually afraid of.

AThat reality itself is a lie — that everything I experience has been constructed to keep me compliant.
BA raid. No warning, no mercy — just the roar of engines and then nothing left.
CBeing identified. Once someone with power decides you're a problem, you're already out of time.
DBeing outmanoeuvred — losing a political game I didn't even know I was playing.
EThe Empire tightening its grip until there's nowhere left to run.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you deal with authority you don't trust?
Every dystopia has a power structure. Your approach to it determines everything.

ASubvert it from the inside — learn its rules well enough to weaponise them against it.
BIgnore it and stay out of its reach. The further from any power structure, the better.
CAppear to comply while doing exactly what I need to do. Visibility is the enemy.
DManoeuvre within it carefully. You can't beat a system you refuse to understand.
EResist openly when I have to. Some things are worth the risk of being seen.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

Which environment could you actually endure long-term?
Survival isn't just tactical — it's physical, psychological, and very much about where you are.

AUnderground bunkers and server rooms — cramped, artificial, but with access to everything that matters.
BOpen wasteland — brutal sun, no shelter, constant movement. At least the threat is honest.
CA dense, rain-soaked city where you can disappear into the crowd and nobody asks questions.
DMerciless desert — extreme heat, no water, and something enormous living beneath the sand.
EThe fringe — backwater planets and busy spaceports where the Empire's attention rarely reaches.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

Who do you want in your corner when things fall apart?
The company you keep is the clearest signal of who you actually are.

AA tight crew of believers who've seen behind the curtain and have nothing left to lose.
BOne or two people I'd trust with my life. Any more than that and someone talks.
CNobody, ideally. Alliances are liabilities. I work alone unless I have no choice.
DA community bound by shared hardship and mutual survival — people who need each other to last.
EA ragtag team with wildly different skills and total commitment when it counts.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

Where do you draw the line — if you draw one at all?
Every survivor eventually faces a moment that tests what they're actually made of.

AI won't harm the innocent — even the ones who'd report me without hesitation.
BI do what I have to to protect the people I've chosen. Everything else is negotiable.
CThe line shifts depending on who's asking and what's at stake.
DI draw a long-term line — nothing that compromises my people's future, even if it'd help now.
ESome lines, once crossed, can't be uncrossed. I know which ones they are.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

What would actually make survival worth it?
Staying alive is one thing. Having a reason to is another.

AWaking others up — dismantling the illusion so no one else has to live inside it.
BFinding somewhere — or someone — worth protecting. A reason to keep moving.
CAnswers. Understanding what I am, what any of this means, before time runs out.
DLegacy — shaping the future in a way that outlasts me by generations.
EFreedom — for myself, for others, for every world still living under someone else's boot.

REVEAL MY WORLD →

Your Fate Has Been Calculated
You'd Survive In…

Your answers point to the world your instincts were built for. This is the universe your temperament, your survival instincts, and your particular brand of stubbornness were made for.

The Resistance, Zion

The Matrix

You took the red pill a long time ago — probably before anyone offered it to you. You're a systems thinker who can't help but notice the seams in things.

You're drawn to understanding how the system works before figuring out how to break it.

You'd find the Resistance, or it would find you — your instinct for spotting constructed realities is the machines' worst nightmare.

You function best when you have access to information and the freedom to act on it.

The Matrix built an airtight prison. You'd be the one probing the walls for the door.

The Wasteland

Mad Max

The wasteland doesn't reward the clever or the well-connected — it rewards those who are hard to kill and harder to break. That's you.

You don't need comfort, community, or a cause larger than the next horizon.

You need a vehicle, a clear threat, and enough fuel to outrun it — and you're good at all three.

You are unsentimental enough to survive that world, and decent enough — just barely — to be something more than another raider.

In the wasteland, that distinction is everything.

Los Angeles, 2049

Blade Runner

You'd survive here because you know how to exist in moral grey areas without losing yourself completely.

You read people accurately, keep your circle small, and ask the questions others prefer not to answer.

In a city where humanity is a legal designation rather than a feeling, you hold onto something that keeps you functional.

You're not a hero. But you're not lost, either.

In Blade Runner's world, that distinction is everything.

Arrakis

Dune

Arrakis is the most hostile environment in the known universe — and you are precisely the kind of person it rewards.

Patience, discipline, and political awareness are your core strengths — and on Arrakis, they're survival tools.

You understand that the long game matters more than any single victory.

Others come to Dune and are consumed by it. You'd learn its logic and earn its respect.

In time, you wouldn't just survive Arrakis — you'd begin to reshape it.

A Galaxy Far, Far Away

Star Wars

The galaxy far, far away is vast, loud, and in a constant state of violent political upheaval — and you wouldn't have it any other way.

You find meaning in being part of something larger than yourself — a cause, a crew, a rebellion.

You'd gravitate toward the Rebellion, or the fringes, or whatever pocket of the galaxy still believes the Empire's grip can be broken.

You fight — not because you have to, but because standing aside isn't something you're capable of.

In Star Wars, that willingness is what makes all the difference.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

Was 'The Beekeeper' Successful?

The movie was well received, and it currently has a 71% critics' score and a "Verified Hot" 92% audience score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "Cheerfully undemanding and enjoyably retrograde, The Beekeeper proves that when it comes to dispensing action-thriller justice, Statham hasn't lost his sting." That enthusiasm translated into ticket sales. Produced for a reported $40 million, The Beekeeper earned approximately $162 million worldwide, making it a substantial commercial success and eventually leading to development of a sequel.

The sequel, The Beekeeper 2, will be released in January 2027, and will be directed by Timo Tjahjanto, with Ayer instead opting to move on to Heart of the Beast. Meanwhile, Statham's Shelter is continuing to redeem itself on streaming following a lackluster box-office run, and his latest release, Mutiny, is still playing in theaters.

The Beekeeper is streaming now on Peacock. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

In The Beekeeper, one man's brutal campaign for vengeance takes on national stakes after he is revealed to be a former operative of a powerful and clandestine organization known as "Beekeepers".

Chris is a Senior News Writer for Collider. He can be found in an IMAX screen, with his eyes watering and his ears bleeding for his own pleasure. He joined the news team in 2022 and accidentally fell upwards into a senior position despite his best efforts.
For reasons unknown, he enjoys analyzing box office receipts, giant sharks, and has become known as the go-to man for all things Bosch, Mission: Impossible and Christopher Nolan in Collider's news division. Recently, he found himself yeehawing along to the Dutton saga on the Yellowstone Ranch.
He is proficient in sarcasm, wit, Photoshop and working unfeasibly long hours. Amongst his passions sit the likes of the history of the Walt Disney Company, the construction of theme parks, steam trains and binge-watching Gilmore Girls with a coffee that is just hot enough to scald him.
His obsession with the Apple TV+ series Silo is the subject of mockery within the Senior News channel, where his feelings about Taylor Sheridan's work are enough to make his fellow writers roll their eyes.

Jason Statham is the most dependable and reliable action star of our generation. Every year, a new Statham action movie comes out, and it delivers exactly what we want: a one-man army, a few quips, some cannon fodder bad guys, and the good guy winning in the end. Sometimes, though, these films hit a bit differently and are elevated because something about them is just better than the norm. In 2024, Statham took on what could have been a silly film with David Ayer, but it became something much bigger. Now, a new audience can see it.

More than two years after becoming a surprise theatrical hit, The Beekeeper has officially found a new streaming home on Peacock. The film features Statham as Adam Clay, a deadly ex-operative of a secret government agency called — you guessed it — the Beekeepers. After a cybercrime ring drives his friend to suicide, Clay launches a relentless, violent crusade for justice. Ayer reportedly brought in a retired FBI agent to consult on the movie’s structure and procedural aspects. Meanwhile, Statham, ever the committed performer, took the time to learn about beekeeping and trained hard for the film’s most demanding stunts — most of which he performed himself.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F6744a68442faa-IMG_9103.PNG?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

The cast is led by Statham as Adam Clay, alongside Emmy Raver-Lampman (The Umbrella Academy) as FBI Agent Verona Parker, Josh Hutcherson (The Hunger Games) as Derek Danforth, Bobby Naderi (Bright) as Matt Wiley, Minnie Driver (Good Will Hunting) as Janet Harward, Phylicia Rashad (Creed) as Eloise Parker, Jemma Redgrave (Doctor Who) as President Danforth, and Jeremy Irons (Watchmen) as Wallace Westwyld.

Collider Exclusive · Sci-Fi Survival Quiz
Which Sci-Fi World Would You Survive?
The Matrix · Mad Max · Blade Runner · Dune · Star Wars

Five universes. Five completely different ways the future went wrong — or sideways, or up in flames. Only one of them is the world your instincts were built for. Eight questions will figure out which dystopia, galaxy, or desert wasteland you'd actually make it out of alive.
💊The Matrix
🔥Mad Max
🌧️Blade Runner
🏜️Dune
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2025/01/instar53540922.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2
🚀Star Wars
TEST YOUR SURVIVAL →

You sense something is deeply wrong with the world around you. What do you do?
The first instinct is often the truest one.

APull on every thread until I understand the system — then figure out how to break it.
BStop asking questions and start stockpiling — food, fuel, weapons. Questions don't keep you alive.
CKeep my head down, observe carefully, and trust no one until I know who's pulling the strings.
DStudy the patterns. Every system has a rhythm — learn it, and you learn how to survive it.
EFind the people fighting back and join them. You can't fix a broken galaxy alone.
NEXT QUESTION →
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2025/01/instar49886674.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=50&h=65&dpr=2

In a world of scarcity, what resource do you guard most fiercely?
What we protect reveals what we believe survival actually requires.

AKnowledge. If you understand the system, you don't need resources — you can generate them.
BFuel. Everything else — movement, power, escape — runs on it.
CTrust. In a world of fakes and informants, a truly reliable ally is rarer than any commodity.
DWater. And after water, information — the two things empires are truly built on.
EShips and credits. The galaxy is big — you survive it by being able to move through it freely.
NEXT QUESTION →

What kind of threat keeps you up at night?
Fear is useful data — if you're honest about what you're actually afraid of.

AThat reality itself is a lie — that everything I experience has been constructed to keep me compliant.
BA raid. No warning, no mercy — just the roar of engines and then nothing left.
CBeing identified. Once someone with power decides you're a problem, you're already out of time.
DBeing outmanoeuvred — losing a political game I didn't even know I was playing.
EThe Empire tightening its grip until there's nowhere left to run.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/12/amazon01_logo-1.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2
NEXT QUESTION →

How do you deal with authority you don't trust?
Every dystopia has a power structure. Your approach to it determines everything.

ASubvert it from the inside — learn its rules well enough to weaponise them against it.
BIgnore it and stay out of its reach. The further from any power structure, the better.
CAppear to comply while doing exactly what I need to do. Visibility is the enemy.
DManoeuvre within it carefully. You can't beat a system you refuse to understand.
EResist openly when I have to. Some things are worth the risk of being seen.
NEXT QUESTION →
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/11/peacock-premium-logo.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2

Which environment could you actually endure long-term?
Survival isn't just tactical — it's physical, psychological, and very much about where you are.

AUnderground bunkers and server rooms — cramped, artificial, but with access to everything that matters.
BOpen wasteland — brutal sun, no shelter, constant movement. At least the threat is honest.
CA dense, rain-soaked city where you can disappear into the crowd and nobody asks questions.
DMerciless desert — extreme heat, no water, and something enormous living beneath the sand.
EThe fringe — backwater planets and busy spaceports where the Empire's attention rarely reaches.
NEXT QUESTION →

Who do you want in your corner when things fall apart?
The company you keep is the clearest signal of who you actually are.

AA tight crew of believers who've seen behind the curtain and have nothing left to lose.
BOne or two people I'd trust with my life. Any more than that and someone talks.
CNobody, ideally. Alliances are liabilities. I work alone unless I have no choice.
DA community bound by shared hardship and mutual survival — people who need each other to last.
EA ragtag team with wildly different skills and total commitment when it counts.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/amc_logo.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2
NEXT QUESTION →

Where do you draw the line — if you draw one at all?
Every survivor eventually faces a moment that tests what they're actually made of.

AI won't harm the innocent — even the ones who'd report me without hesitation.
BI do what I have to to protect the people I've chosen. Everything else is negotiable.
CThe line shifts depending on who's asking and what's at stake.
DI draw a long-term line — nothing that compromises my people's future, even if it'd help now.
ESome lines, once crossed, can't be uncrossed. I know which ones they are.
NEXT QUESTION →

What would actually make survival worth it?
Staying alive is one thing. Having a reason to is another.

AWaking others up — dismantling the illusion so no one else has to live inside it.
BFinding somewhere — or someone — worth protecting. A reason to keep moving.
CAnswers. Understanding what I am, what any of this means, before time runs out.
DLegacy — shaping the future in a way that outlasts me by generations.
EFreedom — for myself, for others, for every world still living under someone else's boot.
REVEAL MY WORLD →

Your Fate Has Been Calculated
You'd Survive In…
Your answers point to the world your instincts were built for. This is the universe your temperament, your survival instincts, and your particular brand of stubbornness were made for.
The Resistance, Zion
The Matrix
You took the red pill a long time ago — probably before anyone offered it to you. You're a systems thinker who can't help but notice the seams in things.
You're drawn to understanding how the system works before figuring out how to break it.
You'd find the Resistance, or it would find you — your instinct for spotting constructed realities is the machines' worst nightmare.
You function best when you have access to information and the freedom to act on it.
The Matrix built an airtight prison. You'd be the one probing the walls for the door.
The Wasteland
Mad Max
The wasteland doesn't reward the clever or the well-connected — it rewards those who are hard to kill and harder to break. That's you.
You don't need comfort, community, or a cause larger than the next horizon.
You need a vehicle, a clear threat, and enough fuel to outrun it — and you're good at all three.
You are unsentimental enough to survive that world, and decent enough — just barely — to be something more than another raider.
In the wasteland, that distinction is everything.
Los Angeles, 2049
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/11/peacock_logo-1.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2
Blade Runner
You'd survive here because you know how to exist in moral grey areas without losing yourself completely.
You read people accurately, keep your circle small, and ask the questions others prefer not to answer.
In a city where humanity is a legal designation rather than a feeling, you hold onto something that keeps you functional.
You're not a hero. But you're not lost, either.
In Blade Runner's world, that distinction is everything.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/11/direct-tv-logo.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2
Arrakis
Dune
Arrakis is the most hostile environment in the known universe — and you are precisely the kind of person it rewards.
Patience, discipline, and political awareness are your core strengths — and on Arrakis, they're survival tools.
You understand that the long game matters more than any single victory.
Others come to Dune and are consumed by it. You'd learn its logic and earn its respect.
In time, you wouldn't just survive Arrakis — you'd begin to reshape it.
A Galaxy Far, Far Away
Star Wars
The galaxy far, far away is vast, loud, and in a constant state of violent political upheaval — and you wouldn't have it any other way.
You find meaning in being part of something larger than yourself — a cause, a crew, a rebellion.
You'd gravitate toward the Rebellion, or the fringes, or whatever pocket of the galaxy still believes the Empire's grip can be broken.
You fight — not because you have to, but because standing aside isn't something you're capable of.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2024/11/spectrum-on-demand-logo.jpg?q=49&fit=contain&w=75&h=75&dpr=2
In Star Wars, that willingness is what makes all the difference.
↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ
Was 'The Beekeeper' Successful?

The movie was well received, and it currently has a 71% critics' score and a "Verified Hot" 92% audience score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "Cheerfully undemanding and enjoyably retrograde, The Beekeeper proves that when it comes to dispensing action-thriller justice, Statham hasn't lost his sting." That enthusiasm translated into ticket sales. Produced for a reported $40 million, The Beekeeper earned approximately $162 million worldwide, making it a substantial commercial success and eventually leading to development of a sequel.

The sequel, The Beekeeper 2, will be released in January 2027, and will be directed by Timo Tjahjanto, with Ayer instead opting to move on to Heart of the Beast. Meanwhile, Statham's Shelter is continuing to redeem itself on streaming following a lackluster box-office run, and his latest release, Mutiny, is still playing in theaters.
The Beekeeper is streaming now on Peacock. Stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

items.title: 'Players got better than we expected': Monster Hunter Wilds DLC director says Capcom is retuning its difficulty standards for the expansion's endgame
items.author: lincoln.carpenter@futurenet.com (Lincoln Carpenter)
items.summary: While Monster Hunter Wilds' performance issues dominated the conversation about its reception on PC, one of the other ongoing sources of player frustration
items.text:
While Monster Hunter Wilds' performance issues dominated the conversation about its reception on PC, one of the other ongoing sources of player frustration was the entry's approach to difficulty. Initially, a number of players thought the game was too much of a sleepwalk—but once later updates started amping up the threat level, many of those same players thought Capcom's solutions were inelegant, relying on arbitrary increases to monster damage.

In an interview with PC Gamer at this year's Tokyo Game Show, Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance director Takuro Hiraoka said Capcom's goal for the base game was to avoid driving away newer players—but he's working to ensure the expansion's endgame will satisfy players who thought its approach to difficulty missed the mark.

(Image credit: Capcom)Speaking via translator, Hiraoka said balancing difficulty is "one of the most challenging things to get right in a game," and his objective—first and foremost—is to prevent a situation where players don't feel like they can finish the game they've purchased, because it's not likely that those players will ever come back.

"In my mind, that's where the difficulty curve should be for Wilds, and I think we achieved that—but the player base was so good and so skilled. We had a bit of a gap in expectations. Maybe players got better than we expected in the intervening years," Hiraoka said. "We've grown the audience greatly since Monster Hunter: World, and that was a game where a lot of players dropped off before finishing the story because it got too hard too quickly. We're trying to tackle that issue, which I see as a problem."

The reception to Wilds' difficulty, he said, has been a learning experience for Capcom, informing how the studio is working to appeal to "not just the hardest of the hardcore" with the Ascendance expansion while making sure challenge-oriented players don't feel alienated by the effort.

(Image credit: Capcom)"We expect that if you purchase the DLC, you're going to want to see as much of the story that we've presented as possible—but for players who want to go far beyond and have the really toughest challenges, we expect that the endgame loop is what really satisfies their needs," Hiraoka said. "We're working on that balance at the minute."

Along similar lines, Hiraoka said that the aggression showcased in Capcom's recent Ascendance weapon breakdown videos shouldn't lead players to believe that they'll be able to completely outclass monsters with their new Boost Bracer attacks. While the videos are edited to highlight the impact of those new mechanics, he said it's "not quite so constant and aggressive" over the course of an actual hunt.

"There is a cadence to it, where the player is building a gauge, keeping an eye on how many charges they have, and deciding when they want to bust out those actions. And you only have a certain amount of time in boost mode whenever you do activate it," Hiraoka said. "Overall, the player hasn't become this hyperaggressive, constant demon mode type of presence. It's a new tool in your box. How to strategize on when to use it, and the way it changes each weapon's gameplay, is for the players to discover."

Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance launches in 2027. You can wishlist the expansion on Steam now.

items.title: Single player games might require age verification if they use Steam under EU Kids Act's current draft, according to MEP's senior policy adviser
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: The European Commission proposed new rules around how under-15s access the likes of social media, AI chatbots, and online video games earlier this week. The
items.text:
The European Commission proposed new rules around how under-15s access the likes of social media, AI chatbots, and online video games earlier this week. The draft legislation is called the EU Kids Act and calls for the setting up of a tiered system governing the types of accounts children under 15 can create to access such services, enforced by mandatory age verification for all users.

The documents laying out the proposal have been officially released, and based on the current wording the Commission have used to define what they class as an online game, it seems single player games that rely on online platforms like Steam for updates, distribution, or even a one-time authentication could be caught in the crossfire. That is, unless the definition is tightened up before the law is set in stone, if it indeed it makes it that far.

When the proposal originally leaked, prior to its official unveiling by European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, reports suggested there was no detail as to how the body had defined the concept of "online games" - and by extension, which sorts of games would fall under the proposed regulations. Now it looks as if that definition is rather broad, as it stands.

For instance, in a press conference held by the Stop Killing Games campaign about the proposed act, European Pirate Party senior policy adviser Paul Diegel - who serves as an assistant to sitting European Parliament member Markéta Gregorová - noted that the current draft of the legislation would even see single player games affected "because they're connected to Steam for updates". Since the proposal docs are publicly available via the European Commission's site, I've dug out the current version of the section on what is or isn't an online game as far as the proposed act is concerned. It reads as follows:

Video games have become an important part of the digital environment in which minors participate and interact with others, in a playful, goal-oriented or entertaining manner. Certain video gaming platforms allow the dissemination and exchange of user-generated content to an indeterminate number of recipients of the service and the facilitation of contact between these recipients. Such online games fall within the definition of online platforms referred to in Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 and should be covered by the scope of this Regulation.

At the same time, some online games that do not allow the dissemination of information to an indeterminate number of recipients should also fall within the scope of this Regulation. This is the case of any game that can be played on a computer, a mobile device, or a games console, irrespective of whether the game underlying software is subsequently executed locally, remotely, such as by means of durable medium, and irrespective of whether the service is provided free of charge, against payment, or against hybrid remuneration involving in-service (or in-application) purchases.

Online games that are accessible or purchasable exclusively through physical media, without any online component enabling their access, distribution, or purchase, are not considered online games for the purposes of this Regulation. For the avoidance of doubt, where an online game also has certain features corresponding to a video sharing platform, it shall be considered an online game for the purpose of this Regulation.

If I'm reading that right, the sole exception in the current proposal applies to games that can only be bought or accessed physically, not via an online storefront like Steam. Even if the online element's only being used to distribute the game and subsequently ship updates to it, it seems like it would fall under the purview of the regulation as it's written at this stage, meaning it'd be subject to age verification.

It's worth noting that the EU Kids Act is still just a proposal at the moment. Tightening up or refining definitions such as this one, so that the law only affects exactly the sorts of games it intends to, is something I'd peg as almost certain to happen as the pending legislation is revised and scrutinised as part of the EU's lawmaking process. That means that if the Act does eventually end up being set into law, it could have a definition that only singles out specific types of online game that mirror social media, in the sense of connecting children to endless other players they can chat with or see the user-created content of.

For now, I'm gonna go and spend what remains of my Friday afternoon writing about a topic less heavy on legal jargon.

items.title: Unbiased Monster Hunter producer predicts one weapon will climb the popularity rankings in Ascendance, has no agenda: 'Hammer should definitely go up a place or two'
items.author: lincoln.carpenter@futurenet.com (Lincoln Carpenter)
items.summary: Over the last two weeks, Capcom dropped a parade of weapon breakdown videos showcasing the new Boost Bracer mechanics coming in the Monster Hunter Wilds:
items.text:
Over the last two weeks, Capcom dropped a parade of weapon breakdown videos showcasing the new Boost Bracer mechanics coming in the Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance expansion. Serving as a sort of on-demand sicko mode, the Boost Bracer lets hunters juice their combat actions with additional speed and impact, and adds some deliciously over-the-top attacks to the existing weapon movesets.

PC Gamer spoke to some of the lead Monster Hunter developers at TGS to pick their brains about how the Boost Bracer evolves the flow of Monster Hunter combat—and which weapon they expected to gain the most fans with its new moves. Asked what weapon they'd stake 10,000 yen on climbing the popularity rankings in Ascendance, one of the developers had an immediate answer.

"Hammer," series producer Ryozo Tsujimoto said without hesitation. "I think the hammer should definitely go up a place or two."

As a hammer main myself, my natural inclination is to cosign Tsujimoto's objective appraisal of the weapon's self-evident efficacy, utility, and inherent nobility. But I'm obligated as a journalist to acknowledge that there might be some slight favoritism in play.

Tsujimoto, who's worked as Monster Hunter series producer since the release of Monster Hunter Freedom 2 in 2007, has a decades-long record as an avowed hammer diehard. At the 2023 Justdan Game Festival in Taiwan, he revealed his Monster Hunter Rise guild card, which confirmed that he'd used the hammer in each and every one of his 895 completed hunts.

Some of the comments claiming favoritism clearly don't know Ryozo is a Hammer main for life. 😂 https://t.co/UZxRuLTH2H pic.twitter.com/DblajWnXunSeptember 14, 2026

He literally doubled down on his hammer devotion in prerelease interviews for Monster Hunter Wilds: Asked by PlayStation Asia how he'd utilize mid-hunt weapon swapping—a new feature in Wilds—he said "both of my weapons will be hammers."

To Tsujimoto's credit, and at the risk of revealing even more of my personal biases, I'll note that the hammer's Boost Bracer toolkit does look pretty sick. In its Ascendance hammer breakdown video, Capcom showed off the return of Rise's Impact Crater switch skill as the new attack that'll let hammer hunters enter boost mode. And once they've engaged sicko status, they'll have access to a mid-charge boost dash for repositioning and closing distance, as well as a brutal new one-armed slam that can follow up the hammer's heaviest charged attacks.

If you suspect this coverage has a compromising pro-hammer slant—and at this point I suppose I can't blame you—Ascendance director Takuro Hiraoka offered a second opinion: While the long sword has always enjoyed its place at the top of the MonHun weapon popularity rankings, he said gunlance will likely win over some converts.
